newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - April 28.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - April 28.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
IMF SOUNDS CURRENCY ALARM

The International Monetary Fund yesterday voiced concern over potential disruption to foreign exchange markets through delays in the introduction of a single European currency. Meanwhile, German finance minister Theo Waigel dismissed concerns that Germany would not meet the criteria for entry on time. The comments came as the G7 nations dealt with problems caused by the strong dollar at their half-yearly meeting in Washington.
SMALL FACTORIES SET FOR FURTHER RISES IN OUTPUT

A survey from the Confederation of British Industry, published today, shows that small and medium-sized manufacturing companies are anticipating further rises in output over the next four months despite worries over the outlook for exports. Increases in orders and output match those of bigger businesses, although the trend in domestic prices and investment is lower.
LLOYD'S REPORT CALLS FOR END TO SYSTEM OF NAMES

Lloyd's of London is today set to approve an end to the system of Names. A working party is expected to stop short of recommending that Names be banned from underwriting with unlimited liability, but to stress that the system be scrapped. Names are attempting to halt the reforms.
THE TIMES
BRITAIN LOSING FOREIGN INVESTMENT TO PRO-EU COUNTRIES

A report from the National Institute of Economic and Social Research has shown that industry is suffering a fall in investment, with foreign firms favouring countries with a strong European Union commitment. The report showed France has overtaken the UK as favorite centre for new investment into the EU by foreign companies.
MILLENNIUM BUG FEARS EXAGGERATED

Taskforce 2000, the government-sponsored agency formed to deal with the millennium computer problem, has admitted that its 31 million pound stg estimate of the cost of the problem to industry was exaggerated. It said the estimate was a means of drawing attention to the problem, rather than a practical estimate.
US ELECTIONS COST BAT $827,000

B.A.T Industries has revealed in a letter to corporate governance lobby group Pirc that it spent $827,000 last year on political donations in the USA. Most were to Republican candidates. The figure is not disclosed to shareholders in the annual report, despite a requirement to detail donations to UK political parties.
THE GUARDIAN
TREASURY ACTUARY ACCUSED

A senior Treasury official, Government actuary Christopher Daykin, is accused of revealing secret details of fund surpluses to help privatise British Coal. He is accused of supplying details in 1991 of a huge surplus in the Mineworks Pension Scheme to British Coal as the corporation prepared for pit closures ahead of privatisation.
SEARS BOSS WINS 500,000 POUND PAYOFF AS PROFITS PLUNGE

Liam Strong is expected to quit as chief executive of Sears with a 500,000 pound stg payoff following the group's profits plunge and the failed attempts to sell the Freeman's mail order business. Non-executive chairman Sir Robert Reid is expected to announce he is taking over, as well as the splitting of the group into three parts. Profits have fallen from 102 million to under 80 million pounds for 1996.
CORRUPTION ON G7 AGENDA

The USA has called for initiative from the G7 industrialised nations to stamp out corruption. The US wants OECD countries to eliminate the tax deductibility of bribes of foreign officials and to criminalise such attempts.
THE INDEPENDENT
GREEN SACKED AS CO-OP FIRES OFF MORE LETTERS

The Co-operative Wholesale Society has gone on the attack over the hostile takeover attempts by Andrew Regan of Lancia Trust. CWS has written to Regan's law firm with accusations of professional misjudgment. A letter has also gone to the London Stock Exchange demanding an enquiry into alleged insider dealing in Lancia Trust. The DTI, the Bank of England and the Serious Fraud Office have also received letters, as have suspended executives Allan Green and David Chambers.
BUSINESS LEADERS DECLARE SUPPORT FOR LABOUR

Seven leading businessmen who have never voted Labour have written an open letter, to be published today, backing Labour and Tony Blair. The letter is a direct response to a letter last week in support of the Conservatives, signed by 38 company chiefs. The seven include Alec Reed of Reed Personnel Services, Alan Sugar of Amstrad, Gerry Robinson of Granada, Sir Trevor Chinn of Lex Service and Ronald Cohen of Apax Partners.
SHAKE-UP AT MEPC MAY LEAD TO SELL-OFFS

Property group MEPC, which recently ended merger discussions with its rival Hammerson, has launched a shake-up after pressure from dissatisfied shareholders following poor performance against rivals like British Land. The proposals could see parts of the group sold off or floated later in the year.
